extracted.intended_audience: federal agency policymakers, lawyers, and staff involved in rulemaking and AI deployment
extracted.subtask_description: Principled guidance for how agencies should deploy large language models in the federal rulemaking process, including what tasks LLMs are suited for, their failure modes, and process safeguards agencies should adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency versus accuracy (statistical plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs generate text that is statistically likely in light of their training data, producing fluent, plausible-sounding outputs that are only loosely correlated with factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize fluent outputs may still contain factual mistakes or omissions and often sound confident regardless of accuracy. Treat fluency as insufficient evidence of correctness; require human verification and cite-checking. Be aware LLMs are stochastic—repeat prompts or vary instructions to detect inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-data coverage limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because LLMs draw upon an enormous corpus of human writing, they are good at topics well represented in training data but may perform poorly on factually specific questions unless relevant materials are provided via prompt or retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide relevant materials through retrieval-augmentation or prompting when answering narrow, fact-specific queries. Do not assume comprehensive knowledge of obscure or unpublished materials. Anticipate reproduction of historical errors or biases present in training data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sycophancy and obedience to user prompts (contextual drift)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs generally do as they are told, tending to tell users what they want to hear, failing to push back, and over time treating user premises as established background (contextual drift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate by system- or exchange-level prompts that instruct models to be forthright, consider competing perspectives, and flag uncertainty. Avoid prompts that embed desired conclusions or prime the model toward a preferred outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate task selection (use-as-subordinate model)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can act like diligent subordinates—reviewing literature, articulating and synthesizing concepts, explaining competing views, structuring thinking, playing devil's advocate, and drafting/sharpening prose. They can also categorize and summarize public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor LLM use for preparatory, analytic, and draft-generation tasks where outputs will be reviewed and incorporated by humans. Do not treat LLM outputs as final; limit their role to assistance rather than decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory human oversight and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any LLM output created in the rulemaking process must be subject to human oversight and validation; individual users can never treat outputs as the final word and outputs must be carefully cite-checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documented human review workflows, senior-level signoff for substantive outputs, and explicit verification steps (e.g., confirm citations, check legal conclusions). Ensure reviewers have time and resources to perform meaningful validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human capacity as rate-limiting factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must ensure staff have the time and bandwidth to actually perform meaningful review; human capacity to oversee LLMs should function as a rate-limiting factor on LLM usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design deployment plans around available review capacity; if LLM output volume would overwhelm staff review, scale back LLM usage or augment verification resources before wider deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match review rigor to potential cost of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should match the review required to the potential costs of an LLM mistake: higher-stakes tasks that directly inform regulatory substance require additional safeguards and senior review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tasks that could produce adverse real-world consequences or affect legal sufficiency of rules, require extra layers of human review, possibly by more experienced staff or multiple reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use LLMs when verification is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not elicit or use LLM outputs when verification is impracticable—i.e., when the effort to verify equals or exceeds the effort to do the underlying analysis without AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If verifying an LLM's conclusion would require recreating its work or an amount of effort comparable to doing the analysis directly (for example, assessing consistency with all relevant precedent), avoid relying on the LLM for that task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation and backtesting for comment summarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Because agencies must adequately respond to significant comments, LLM-produced comment summaries must be accurate and complete, and agencies should develop tests of typical LLM comment-review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible tests: use LLMs to summarize past rulemaking comment records and compare to agency analyses; cross-check LLM summaries on new rules against an independent sample of comments the agency deems significant. If reliable validation is impracticable, avoid using LLMs for comment-response work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompting best practices (e.g., identify counterarguments, flag uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs should be asked to identify substantial counterarguments and objections, flag uncertainty and contested claims, and canvass competing schools of thought before reaching conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed these instructions in system prompts and individual exchanges. Avoid prompts that prime the model toward a desired conclusion. Use explicit instructions to surface alternative views and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt transparency and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency policymakers and lawyers reviewing an LLM output should have before them the prompts used to generate it so that priming, sycophancy, and biases are visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain records of prompts, system instructions, and key configuration parameters alongside generated outputs for review, auditing, and potential litigation discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against automation bias and rubber-stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: There is risk that oversight becomes pro forma—officials may rubber-stamp LLM outputs, fall prey to automation bias, or otherwise fail to perform rigorous verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedural checks to ensure active engagement (e.g., requirement to annotate specific verification steps), rotate reviewers, and train staff to resist overreliance on AI-generated analysis to avoid erosion of analytic capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate cognitive offloading and skill erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Overreliance on LLMs for intellectual work (cognitive offloading) might erode agency staff analytic capabilities and habit of critical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve opportunities for staff to perform core analytic tasks without AI, require manual drafting or review for certain workstreams, and monitor for decline in institutional expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for model stochasticity (multiple runs and variation checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs are stochastic; the same prompt can yield different outputs at different times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt models more than once or with slightly different instructions to detect uncertainty or inconsistency; treat agreement across multiple outputs as increased confidence and variation as a signal to scrutinize further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit ambitious automation of rulemaking tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to automate the vast majority of work on a particular rulemaking task (e.g., rescinding half of regulations automatically) should be viewed with extreme skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design LLM workflows to preclude wholesale automation of substantive regulatory decisionmaking; ensure genuine human review and meaningful design requirements that prevent mass delegation to LLMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop internal processes and senior oversight analogous to managing junior staff
rubrics_metrics.description: LLM deployments should be overseen like the work of fallible subordinates: proper instructions, attentive oversight, and matching review to task risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build formal processes for verification, designate responsible senior reviewers, require documentation of who reviewed and why, and ensure that oversight practices are enforced rather than nominal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mitigation techniques (retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods like retrieval-augmented generation and chain-of-thought prompting may improve the accuracy of LLM responses, though it is unclear which model flaws are systemic and which will recede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these technical mitigations as part of layered safeguards but do not assume they eliminate systemic risks; validate empirically in agency contexts before broad reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of reproducing biases and embedded errors
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs may reproduce errors or biases embodied in their training data and the historical framing of policy problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt evenhandedness measures (e.g., instruct models to canvass competing perspectives), monitor outputs for biased framings, and use prompt transparency plus human review to detect and correct bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of broader legal and democratic values
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment decisions should be informed by other concerns—administrative-law doctrines, democratic accountability, deliberation, transparency, due process, public participation, and the appropriateness of private-company-controlled tools in policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat procedural and normative questions (legal sufficiency, accountability, transparency, equity) as part of the decision whether and how to use LLMs; these issues may require separate legal and policy analysis beyond technical safeguards.
